name: Search-Based Reasoning
question: Should I try several paths before committing?
summary: Instead of committing to one line of reasoning, the model proposes several candidate thoughts at each step, a value function scores them, and a search (breadth-first, depth-first or Monte Carlo tree search) expands the promising ones and backs out of dead ends. Tree of Thoughts applies this to reasoning; LATS adds tool actions, environment feedback and reflection.
useCases: Early wrong choices commit you and are costly to undo
There is a reliable way to score partial solutions
Accuracy matters more than cost or latency

steps.title: Propose k candidate thoughts
steps.text: From the depot, the model proposes k = 3 possible first stops: the hospital, the pharmacy or the cold-chain drop. Each is one small, checkable step.

steps.title: Evaluate each candidate
steps.text: A value prompt rates each partial route as sure, likely or impossible, mapped to 20, 1 and 0.001 as in the Tree of Thoughts code. Pharmacy first is impossible: it opens after the hospital's deadline.

steps.title: Select the best b
steps.text: Only the top b = 2 candidates survive: hospital first (sure) and cold-chain first (likely). The impossible branch is dropped, so no more calls are spent on it.

steps.title: Expand level by level
steps.text: Each kept route gets 3 new proposals, so the second level has 6 candidates. The search repeats propose, evaluate and select until the depth limit.

steps.title: Prune dead ends
steps.text: Two of the six second-level routes break a time window and are pruned. The surviving branch from the hospital reaches a valid route at depth 3.

steps.title: MCTS variant: balance value and exploration
steps.text: Monte Carlo tree search, as in LATS, picks which node to expand with UCT: average value plus an exploration bonus that is largest for rarely visited nodes. Unvisited nodes go first.

practice.scenario: A logistics firm in Pune sequences multi-drop deliveries for vans with time windows: a hospital before 10:00, a pharmacy after 11:00, a cold-chain drop within 40 minutes of loading. A single chain of reasoning often commits to a bad first stop. A breadth-first search proposes three next stops at each step, scores partial routes with a checker, keeps the best two and prunes routes that already break a window.

practice.note: The first file is a plain-Python BFS you can adapt; propose and value stand for model calls (or a checker). The second runs the reference package on Game of 24 and needs an OpenAI API key.

samples.code:
def bfs(start, k=3, b=2, depth=4):
    frontier = [start]                                   # partial routes
    calls = 0
    for _ in range(depth):
        candidates = []
        for state in frontier:
            for nxt in propose(state, k):                # k thoughts per state
                calls += 1
                candidates.append((value(state + [nxt]), state + [nxt]))
        candidates = [c for c in candidates if c[0] > 0]  # prune impossible
        candidates.sort(key=lambda c: c[0], reverse=True)
        frontier = [route for _, route in candidates[:b]] # keep the beam
        if not frontier:
            return None, calls
    return frontier[0], calls

numericDrill.question: A breadth-first search uses k = 3 proposals per state, beam b = 2 and depth d = 3. Each proposal costs one call to generate and one call to evaluate. Level 1 expands only the root; later levels expand the 2 kept states. How many model calls does the search make in total?
numericDrill.answer: Level 1: 1 × 3 = 3 proposals, 6 calls. Levels 2 and 3: 2 × 3 = 6 proposals each, 12 calls each. Total 6 + 12 + 12 = 30 calls, against 3 for a single chain of depth 3.

interview.question: When is Tree of Thoughts worth its cost?
interview.answer: When an early wrong choice commits you to a dead end and there is a reliable way to score partial solutions, as in puzzles, planning and code with tests. If a single chain already succeeds, or you cannot evaluate partial states, the extra calls are wasted.

interview.question: How does self-consistency relate to tree search?
interview.answer: Self-consistency samples several complete reasoning chains and takes a majority vote on the final answer. It is breadth without intermediate scoring or backtracking, so it is cheaper and simpler, but it cannot prune a bad path halfway through.

mistakes.mistake: Raising k and b without checking the evaluator
mistakes.fix: Test the value function first; a noisy judge prunes good branches

mistakes.mistake: Searching tasks a single chain already solves
mistakes.fix: Measure a single chain first and search only the failures

quiz.question: A delivery planner often commits to a bad first stop that makes later time windows impossible. Which approach fits?
options: A single chain with a longer prompt
Tree search: propose several next stops, score them and back out of dead ends
Voting on the final route only
quiz.explanation: When early choices commit you, exploring and scoring several branches beats a single chain.

quiz.question: A BFS uses k = 3 proposals, beam b = 2 and depth 3. Each proposal costs one generate and one evaluate call. Level 1 expands only the root. How many calls in total?
quiz.explanation: Level 1: 3 proposals, 6 calls. Levels 2 and 3: 2 × 3 = 6 proposals, 12 calls each. Total 30.

quiz.question: On Game of 24 with GPT-4, what success rates did the Tree of Thoughts paper report for chain of thought and ToT?
quiz.explanation: Chain of thought solved 4%; Tree of Thoughts solved 74%.

quiz.question: A UCT function returns exploit − explore. What happens?
options: Unexplored nodes are penalised, so the search keeps expanding the same branch
quiz.explanation: The exploration bonus must be added; subtracting it discourages exploring rarely visited nodes.

quiz.question: With a noisy value prompt, a search keeps losing the right branch. Which changes help? Select all that apply.
options: Widen the beam so more states survive
Improve the value function, for example with a rule-based checker
Raise k while keeping a beam of 1
Reduce depth below what the problem needs
quiz.explanation: A wider beam or a better evaluator keeps the right branch. More proposals with a narrow beam, or too little depth, do not.

quiz.question: Self-consistency samples several reasoning chains and takes a majority vote. What does it lack compared with Tree of Thoughts?
options: Scoring and pruning of intermediate steps
quiz.explanation: Self-consistency votes on final answers; it cannot prune a bad path halfway through.

quiz.question: LATS reported what pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4?
quiz.explanation: LATS combined MCTS, an LM value function and reflection to reach 92.7% pass@1 on HumanEval.

quiz.question: In the Tree of Thoughts code, which value mapping is used for sure, likely and impossible?
quiz.explanation: The Game of 24 value prompt maps sure to 20, likely to 1 and impossible to 0.001.

quiz.question: A scheduling search for operating theatres is too expensive. Which reduce model calls? Select all that apply.
options: Lower k where the right step is usually a top proposal
Prune impossible states early with a cheap code check
Increase depth beyond what the schedule needs
quiz.explanation: Fewer proposals and early pruning cut calls. A wider beam and extra depth multiply them.

quiz.question: A single chain of depth 3 costs 6 calls (generate and evaluate per step). A search that solves the task costs 30. When is the search worth it?
options: When the chain fails often and a failure is costly
Always, because it is more thorough
Never, because it costs five times as much
quiz.explanation: Search pays off when a single chain fails often and mistakes are expensive; otherwise the extra calls are waste.

quiz.question: A BFS uses k = 4, beam b = 3, depth 2, with one generate and one evaluate call per proposal. How many calls?
quiz.explanation: Level 1: 4 proposals, 8 calls. Level 2: 3 × 4 = 12 proposals, 24 calls. Total 32.

quiz.question: Which are Tree of Thoughts search settings in the official code? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: n_generate_sample and n_select_sample (with n_evaluate_sample) control the ToT search. max_turns and budget_tokens belong to other tools.

quiz.question: Self-consistency improved chain of thought on GSM8K by about how much in its paper?
quiz.explanation: The paper reports a +17.9% gain on GSM8K from majority voting over sampled chains.

quiz.question: A route search’s right third stop is only the model’s 3rd most likely proposal. With k = 2, what happens regardless of the beam?
options: The right route is never found
quiz.explanation: If the right step is never proposed, no amount of beam or scoring can keep it.

quiz.question: Which signs suggest search is the wrong tool? Select all that apply.
options: A single chain already solves 98% of cases
There is no way to score a partial solution
Early mistakes are costly and hard to undo
A reliable checker for partial states exists
quiz.explanation: If chains already work or partial states cannot be scored, search adds cost for little gain. The other two favour search.

quiz.question: In MCTS with UCT, an unvisited child is usually given what score?
options: Infinite, so it is tried first
quiz.explanation: Unvisited children get top priority so every option is tried at least once.

quiz.question: Search spends compute on breadth outside the model. Which spends extra compute inside a single call instead?
options: A larger thinking budget on a reasoning model
quiz.explanation: Reasoning models think within one call; voting, beam search and MCTS make many calls.

quiz.question: A search with 5 proposals per state and beam 2 examines how many candidates at level 3, if levels 2 and 3 each expand the 2 kept states?
quiz.explanation: Each level after the first expands b × k = 2 × 5 = 10 candidates.

quiz.question: LATS combines which ideas? Select all that apply.
options: A fixed prompt chain with no search
quiz.explanation: LATS uses MCTS with an LM value function, environment feedback and self-reflection.

quiz.question: With a noisy evaluator, raising k from 3 to 5 while keeping b = 2 changed nothing except cost. Why?
options: The right branch was already proposed but the evaluator ranked it below the beam
k has no effect on cost
quiz.explanation: More proposals cannot help if the evaluator keeps dropping the right one; widen the beam or fix the evaluator.
